question: Which statement about Dijkstra's single-source shortest-path algorithm is correct?
options: Dijkstra's algorithm is correct when all edge weights are non-negative; it finalizes the minimum-distance unvisited vertex, and with a binary-heap priority queue runs in O((V + E) log V).
Dijkstra's algorithm also works on graphs with negative edge weights as long as there is no negative cycle, because every outgoing edge of a finalized vertex is relaxed.
Dijkstra's algorithm always takes Θ(V²) time, regardless of the priority queue, because extract-minimum must scan the whole unvisited set at every iteration.
For a single target, Dijkstra's algorithm may stop as soon as the target receives a finite tentative distance, before it is extracted as the minimum.
gold_answer: Dijkstra's algorithm is correct when all edge weights are non-negative; it finalizes the minimum-distance unvisited vertex, and with a binary-heap priority queue runs in O((V + E) log V).
notes: Quoted passages come from the linked Wikipedia and cp-algorithms pages, read live on 2026-11-19. Both sites publish under CC BY-SA 4.0. Re-check the quoted sentences against the live pages before freezing.

positions.answer: Dijkstra's algorithm also works on graphs with negative edge weights as long as there is no negative cycle, because every outgoing edge of a finalized vertex is relaxed.

claims.text: Dijkstra's algorithm stays correct on graphs with negative edge weights provided there is no negative cycle.

evidence.text: The base case is when there is just one visited node, source. Its distance is defined to be zero, which is the shortest distance, since negative weights are not allowed. Hence, the hypothesis holds.
evidence.notes: Quoted from the Proof, Base case subsection.

evidence.text: Since the edges' weights are non-negative, the length of the shortest path l[p] (which we just proved to be equal to d[p]) does not exceed the length l[v] of the shortest path to the vertex v.

claims.verdict_rationale: Both passages make non-negative weights an explicit precondition of the correctness argument; the Wikipedia proof states that negative weights are not allowed, which refutes the claimed extension.

claims.text: A negative edge leaving an already-finalized vertex cannot make that vertex's recorded distance non-minimal.

evidence.text: In the former case, let w be the first unvisited node on this shorter path. By induction, the shortest paths from source to u and w through visited nodes only have costs dist[u] and dist[w] respectively. This means the cost of going from source to u via w has the cost of at least dist[w] + the minimal cost of going from w to u. As the edge costs are non-negative, the minimal cost of going from w to u is a non-negative number.
evidence.notes: Faithfully excerpted from the Proof, Induction subsection.

evidence.text: After any vertex v becomes marked, the current distance to it d[v] is the shortest, and will no longer change.

claims.verdict_rationale: The induction step only rules out a shorter path because it assumes non-negative edge costs; with a negative edge the argument fails, so the passages undercut rather than establish the claim.

claims.text: Uniform cost search, a variant of Dijkstra's algorithm, is guaranteed to beat breadth-first search on unit-weight graphs.

evidence.text: In many fields, particularly artificial intelligence, Dijkstra's algorithm or a variant offers a uniform cost search and is formulated as an instance of the more general idea of best-first search.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage mentions uniform cost search and best-first search but says nothing about breadth-first search, unit weights, or any efficiency comparison, so it cannot establish the claim.

positions.answer: Dijkstra's algorithm always takes Θ(V²) time, regardless of the priority queue, because extract-minimum must scan the whole unvisited set at every iteration.

claims.text: Dijkstra's algorithm always takes Θ(V²) time, whichever priority queue is used.

evidence.text: With a self-balancing binary search tree or binary heap, the algorithm requires Θ((|E|+|V|)log|V|) time in the worst case; for connected graphs this time bound can be simplified to Θ(|E|log|V|). The Fibonacci heap improves this to Θ(|E|+|V|log|V|).
evidence.notes: Quoted from the Running time section.

evidence.text: However in sparse graphs, when m is much smaller than the maximal number of edges n², the problem can be solved in O(n log n + m) complexity.

claims.verdict_rationale: Both passages give bounds better than Θ(V²) for heap-based and sparse-graph implementations, so they deny that the running time is always quadratic.

claims.text: The Θ(V²) bound arises because extract-minimum is a linear scan over the unvisited set.

evidence.text: The simplest version of Dijkstra's algorithm stores the vertex set Q as a linked list or array, and edges as an adjacency list or matrix. In this case, extract-minimum is simply a linear search through all vertices in Q, so the running time is Θ(|E|+|V|²)=Θ(|V|²).
evidence.notes: Quoted from the Running time section.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage directly links the linear-search extract-minimum of the simplest implementation to the Θ(|V|²) running time.

claims.text: The Fibonacci-heap implementation of Dijkstra's algorithm is worst-case optimal on sparse graphs.

evidence.text: For the simplest implementation of these operations on each iteration vertex search requires O(n) operations, and each relaxation can be performed in O(1). Hence, the resulting asymptotic behavior of the algorithm is: O(n²+m). This complexity is optimal for dense graph, i.e. when m ≈ n².
evidence.notes: Faithfully excerpted from the Implementation section.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage discusses optimality for dense graphs and never mentions Fibonacci heaps or sparse-graph optimality, so the cited evidence does not establish the claim.

positions.answer: Dijkstra's algorithm is correct when all edge weights are non-negative; it finalizes the minimum-distance unvisited vertex, and with a binary-heap priority queue runs in O((V + E) log V).

claims.text: Dijkstra's algorithm computes correct shortest paths when every edge weight is non-negative.

evidence.text: Dijkstra's algorithm is commonly used on graphs where the edge weights are non-negative integers or real numbers.

You are given a directed or undirected weighted graph with n vertices and m edges. The weights of all edges are non-negative. You are also given a starting vertex s. This article discusses finding the lengths of the shortest paths from a starting vertex s to all other vertices, and output the shortest paths themselves.

claims.verdict_rationale: Both passages state the non-negative-weight setting for which the algorithm is defined and used to find shortest paths from a source.

claims.text: With a self-balancing binary search tree or binary heap as the priority queue, Dijkstra's algorithm runs in Θ((|E| + |V|) log |V|) worst-case time.

evidence.text: With a self-balancing binary search tree or binary heap, the algorithm requires Θ((|E|+|V|)log|V|) time in the worst case; for connected graphs this time bound can be simplified to Θ(|E|log|V|). The Fibonacci heap improves this to Θ(|E|+|V|log|V|).
evidence.notes: Quoted from the Running time section.

evidence.text: Although Dijkstra's algorithm is optimal for graphs with non-negative edge weights, its practical runtime depends on both data structures and graph properties. Using a binary heap results in a running time of O((V+E)logV).
evidence.notes: Quoted from the Practical performance considerations section.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passages state the same heap-based bound, once as Θ((|E|+|V|) log |V|) worst case and once as O((V+E) log V), which entails the claim.

claims.text: For a single target, Dijkstra's algorithm stops once the target is selected as the current minimum-distance vertex.

evidence.text: If the unvisited set is empty, or contains only nodes with infinite distance (which are unreachable), then the algorithm terminates by skipping to step 6. If the only concern is the path to a target node, the algorithm terminates once the current node is the target node.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage states that for a single target the algorithm terminates when the current node, which step 3 defines as the minimum-distance unvisited node, is the target.
